variants.name: MapStruct annotation-processor mapper (POJOs)
variants.idiom_name: MapStruct @Mapper generated bean mapping (plus Jackson and middleware converters)
variants.implementation_notes: Java's translator is generated or registered, not hand-written: a MapStruct @Mapper interface with @Mapping(source = ..., target = ...) methods is turned into a compile-time implementation, Jackson covers the wire-format half through StdConverter/custom JsonSerializer subclasses, and messaging middleware finds the converter by type instead of by name (Camel's @Converter methods, Spring Integration transformer endpoints). What replaces the classic structure is that interface plus the annotation processor, or the framework's converter registry; a hand-written translator is still justified when the mapping is stateful (loaded code lists) or when several wire versions share one endpoint.
pitfalls: MapStruct's default unmappedTargetPolicy is WARN, so target fields the mapping forgets are dropped with a build note; set ReportingPolicy.ERROR so an unmapped property fails the build.

A Jackson converter or serializer registered for a supertype is not used for subtypes unless ModifierRegistration is explicit, and throwing from a converter aborts the whole response instead of producing an invalid-message route.

Hand-written converter methods with the same source/target pair registered in Camel/Spring win silently over generated ones; duplicate conversions for one pair are a common source of version-mismatch bugs.

variants.name: Jackson converter at the wire boundary
variants.implementation_notes: When the translation is a property-level wire concern, implement StdConverter<Source, Target> (or a JsonSerializer) and register it on the ObjectMapper or with @JsonSerialize; Jackson then applies the translation wherever that property is serialised. Choose it when the boundary is JSON/XML through Jackson and a generated mapper would duplicate what the serializer already drives.
pitfalls: Converters run inside the serialisation pass: an exception escapes as a 500 rather than an invalid-message event, and a converter on a property of a lazy proxy can trigger unexpected loading.
Registering the converter only locally (on a field) leaves other code paths untranslated; the same model then serialises in two different shapes.

variants.name: Records with compact constructors and explicit factory methods
variants.idiom_name: record + compact canonical constructor + of()/from() factories
variants.implementation_notes: With records (Java 16+) the canonical model is a record whose compact constructor validates and normalises invariants, and the translation becomes a static factory LegacyOrder: from(LegacyOrder) / toLegacy() pair; MapStruct and Jackson both understand records, so the generated or reflective path keeps working on them. Prefer this on a modern LTS when you want the validation to be part of the target type instead of a separate translator stage.
pitfalls: Records expose their components reflectively, so a rename changes the JSON wire form unless the names are pinned with @JsonProperty/@Mapping.
Compact-constructor validation makes construction throw, so deserialisation of a malformed message fails inside Jackson rather than at a translator boundary you control.
